conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-traveled questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers; we just want to be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—like yesterday my husband made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper and I cracked up. It maybe takes a tiny bit more effort than before I was pregnant, but the funny side of things is definitely still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

That’s good to hear. Most of the time I still can—like when the baby lets out a big burp right as I’m trying to burp him, I can’t help but giggle. Every so often I’m just too tired to find things funny, but overall I’m still laughing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once the baby’s down for his first nap, or meeting my mom for a walk later this week. They’re small things, but I genuinely enjoy them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If he spits up a ton after I feed him, I might think “maybe I burped him wrong,” but the feeling passes in a minute and I don’t keep beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I catch myself worrying that the baby’s breathing sounds different or that his fever might come back even though the pediatrician said he’s fine. It’s not constant—just little spurts that pop up out of nowhere and then fade once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicky feeling. I get a quick flutter of worry now and then, but it’s not the same as being scared or panicky—it’s more like a fleeting “what if?” and then it’s gone.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m keeping up fine—laundry, feedings, a quick shower, all manageable. Every once in a while, if he’s had a rough night, I’ll think “wow, this is a lot,” but it passes once I nap when he naps.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay. I’m tired when I go to bed, but once the baby settles I can fall asleep pretty easily and stay asleep until he needs the next feed.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt truly sad or miserable. I might get a little emotional when a lullaby makes me tear up, but it’s brief and not that heavy, down feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all—maybe a couple of tears when I was overtired last week, but it was just for a minute and then I was fine.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

It sounds as though you're settling into new motherhood with healthy moments of joy and only the usual fatigue. You still laugh at your baby's funny noises, look forward to small pleasures like coffee during nap-time, and generally feel you're coping, even if occasional worries about the baby's breathing or brief self-blame about burping pop up and quickly fade. You denied persistent sadness, panicky feelings, sleep disruption, or any thoughts of self-harm, and you report only a single tearful moment when overtired.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 6, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes discrete, recurrent worries without medical basis that arise spontaneously and then subside, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 6 falls well below the 9-point cut-off where depression becomes possible. You endorsed only two items at the "sometimes" level: Q4 (anxiety without medical cause) and Q3 (brief self-blame). You denied core <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> criteria such as daily low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, fatigue beyond infant-care demands, sleep disruption unrelated to night feeds, thoughts of self-harm, or panic attacks. The described worries are short-lived and situation-specific, consistent with normal postpartum vigilance rather than an <med>anxiety disorder</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine paediatric and postpartum check-ups
2. Re-screen with EPDS at the six-week visit or sooner if mood, anxiety, or functioning decline
3. Maintain sleep hygiene: nap when baby naps, share night duties where possible
4. Use brief relaxation techniques (slow breathing, grounding exercises) when unsolicited worries appear
5. Stay connected with supportive adults and consider parent-and-baby groups for shared experience
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire, 2 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient, situational worry about infant health (Q4, Q5) – no panic attacks.  
• Occasional “this is a lot” thought after rough night (Q6) – resolves with rest.  

Symptoms denied  
• Persistent low mood, crying spells, anhedonia, guilt/self-blame, sleep-mood link, self-harm ideation (Q1–3, Q7–10).

Pattern  
Overall affective tone is positive; stressors appear normative for new motherhood. No evidence of sustained depressive or anxiety symptoms meeting clinical threshold. No safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Current responses place patient below cut-off for probable major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety disorder. Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if mood, anxiety, or functioning deteriorates.
